It's a puzzle game, much like Islanders, where you work to place buildings on limited space in order to optimize resource production. It's also similar to "Against the Storm", in its roguelike meta-progression. Each area has a time limit, and if you escape in time you go to the cycle map. The time limit carries over to the cycle map, allowing you to pick between new areas and events. You'll pick up artifacts, giving you bonuses, and build out your building deck along the way. Once the cycle time-limit is up, you're transported back to the main hub. You'll use special resources you've collected to unlock new buildings, new bonuses for your next runs, etc. There's also a over-arching story, but personally I'm not a fan. I rather dig into the meat of the game, with lore provided in obscure bits and off-to-the-side (like in Against the Storm). Overall, great puzzle game, great mechanics, definitely worth the asking price. The devs should be proud of what they've accomplished, and I'm excited to see where it goes from here.

A pleasant combination of Against the Storm and Pirates Outlaws: a fast-paced deckbuilder city-building rogue-lite where you chose to navigate various random routes in between the settlements you build on the islands. Before departing on a run you start at your base of operations; which you can decorate, build improvements at which give you permanent boosts for your runs, and where you can unlock new relics. Building the settlements revolves less around resource-management (like in Against the Storm) and more around placement and the combination of various buildings. I have a soft spot for this specific genre of games, so naturally I've had a blast so far. I haven't encountered many bugs yet and the game is already extremely polished and well-rounded. Definitely worth it's money!
Even though you're constantly facing the end of the world, this game can get pretty cozy once you get its rhythm.

Played for 2.5 hours straight after purchase... Giving me slay the spire vibes but the cards are different types of buildings instead. While there's some resource management to the game, it's not as intense as Against The Storm currently. Only gripe I have thus far is that building placement seems to be very crucial in this game, I wish that the developers would soon implement a grid/snap-to-grid system to improve QOL. Looking forward to more updates, definitely has the potential for long replayability! As a person that enjoys slay the spire, against the storm, and frostpunk, Roots of Yggdrasil is right up my alley. While it has similarities, it is also unique in its own way that differentiates from others in the same genre.

Manavoid does it again! So many great things to say about this game! Aside from some minor grammatical errors, it truly had us scratching our heads to come up with constructive feedback. Visually and mechanically compelling. We loved the visual-novel-like look and feel of the characters, the mix of 2D/3D graphics in the environment, and the ever evolving underlying narrative. We're sadly not very well-versed in our Norse Mythology, but even for us, we liked how the game incoperates the folklore both visually and mechanically through loops, scions, the Ginnungagap (which we'll never be able to properly pronounce), and so much more. The card-based city-building mechanic was easy to pick up and quickly had us strategically respecting exploration and the amount of space we had available. Adventures were clever and unique, threats kept us on our toes, and the Holt gave us that much more ability to upgrade and customize. All said, and especially at this price point, this is a very fun and well made game that we'd definitely recommend! TWITCH: Twitch.tv/NerdLovesGeek TWITTER: Twitter.com/Nerd_Loves_Geek

I normally give a thumbs up with an emphasis on honest criticism when reviewing/recommending Early Access games with potential. This time I will give a thumbs down because I do not understand the 98% Very Positive rating on this game with 60 reviews. The game has potential, but gets repetitive very quickly. Building my deck doesnt challenge me with any tactical choice of any significance. I went to the "endgame" twice in my playtime so far (6.6 hours at time of review) and basically have been told "DO IT AGAIN, I SAY SO" by the game ... just because the game actually needs to tell you that to keep you playing. In the end, once I got used to the best (and only) play style I needed to learn to master this game, the biggest challenge became esthetical for me, for I do pride myself on a neatly laid out settlement. 6.5/10 for me.

It's a great foundation for a potentially lovely game. The city building is very similar to Islanders, mixed with the typical roguelike shenanigans of Slay The Spire. The only thing holding it back is a need for increased diversity in buildings, building type combos and natural resource types. Which is not unexpected for an Early Access game. I'm excited to see what comes next!

[h1] A Card Game KING review [/h1] Roots of Yggdrasil is a rare roguelite deckbuilder/basebuilder hybrid that tasks the player with a simple mission of saving the world. If I would have to briefly describe the game, I would say that it's a game that's very light on deckbuilding, cardplay and base building elements but somehow still enjoyable to play, especially if you are looking something more relaxing. Mechanically, players are given a deck of cards, representing buildings, each increasing one of the few resource types when built. You occasionally add new cards to your deck, which are usually new buildings that generate resources in a different way and under different conditions and sometimes manipulate other things (like drawing cards). To complete an island (there are few islands per run) the player must essentially gather enough of specific resources which varies island to island. It's a rather simple gameplay and while I didn't find the deckbuilding or card combo aspect to be deep or even that varied, there is still a sense of satisfaction when placing your buildings just the right way and squeezing the most out of building combo bonuses. There are some downsides to the game too, which I hope to be addressed before release. I didn't find there to be much decision making turn by turn. You would either draw the cards you need and play them or if not skip a turn until you do. Sometimes drawing conditional cards early that require a certain set up can feel very bad and unlucky and with draw being rare, being dealt a bad starting hand feels extra bad (but not game breaking). I've also found the game to lack fun card play - there aren't that many satisfying card combos you can do as the cards themselves typically only ever generate resources. I wished there were more cards that affect other aspects of the game or have fun combos. Lastly, when scouting sometimes it's counterintuitive how paths are connected. One time I was trying to reach an important building that was right next to me, but it turned out it took much more scouting to get to the building. That being said, I still had fun with the game and hope that EA will address some of the issues above. [h1][b]The positive[/b] [/h1] + Simple but satisfying gameplay loop. + Deckbuilding and basebuilding hybrid incorporating the core of each genre. + Permanent upgrades allow for a sense of progression. + Interesting story. [h1][b]The neutral[/b][/h1] * Unintuitive paths. It's not always obvious how the important island buildings are connected. * When zoming out to full, icons of buildings disappear which is a shame because it would be helpful to see them, especially when zoomed out. [h1][b]The negative[/b][/h1] - Needs more interesting cards, effects or interactions. While the gameplay loop is satisfying, long term it might suffer from lack of diversity and repetitiveness. But hopefully this will be improved during the EA. - A bit too slow unlocks for new characters/cards for my taste. [h1][b]Conclusion:[/b] [/h1] A deckbuilding/basebuilding hybrid best enjoyed as a casual past time, but may need more interesting cards/mechanics to stave off repetitiveness. Recommended. Yes, but prepare for a learning curve longer than the 2h refund window. There is a lot of Stuff here. Deck builder smash together with a city builder wrap in a narrative rogue like. You build cities on island in hopes to achieve objectives to collect seeds. Once you have 2-3 of them you move on to the next island. I have played a lot of city builder but this one was the most confusing. there is so many objectives and so many ways to complete seeds that I wasn't sure which ones where necessary of side quest. The game needs a longer more in depth tutorial. It is a Beautiful game with great music and impossible to pronounce words. Once you understands the relationship between buildings and how they connect to get the seeds it all make sense. Yes you will start over and over again but that's the genre, and the game keep it fresh by randomizing the islands and adding new cards and new narrative encounters. There is also the Holt, your base of operation where you can put building that will give you bonus at the beginning of your next loop, make you a little bit stronger every time. In term of Early Access the game is almost bug free for me and could be launch right now and would be in a better state than 90% of the EA out there.

This game scratches all kinds of itches. I tried Against the Storm, but found it a bit more hardcore than I felt like putting effort into. Roots of Yggdrasil is hits the sweet spot for me as a deep but chill resource/expansion race-against-time game. Bottom line: it's thoughtful and fun to play. You should play it too! Gameplay-wise, imagine ISLANDERS, Slay the Spire, Against the Storm, and Northgard were all cooked together. This leads to a somewhat bonkers mix of genres, where you have a deck-builder rogue-lite node-travelling resource-management city builder. It's very intuitive and all works reasonably well together. Aesthetically, you have your standard steampunk viking aesthetic (!) where you lay telephone wire between magic trees and try to power up your flying longship. I loved the visual design of the environments and side-characters, although found some of the main characters a bit YA. They're a bit lightweight compared to the far more interesting characters you meet out in the world. (Your crew bickers a lot. Not all that endearing or interesting, to be honest.) Downsides: not a lot of graphical options for potato computers. Feels a bit grindy for the meta-progression (three different currency acorns for upgrades that scale up in cost fast), without a plot to justify what's straightforwardly called the "loop" of the game. The homebase upgrades are finicky to place. The game feels a bit cramped on a laptop screen. All in all, it feels like a bunch of Devs grew up in the golden age of Indie Games and spun that into a great game. It has flexible systems that feel good to play around with. I've had great comebacks, last-minute escapes, broken combos, and heartbreaking losses. It's a serious, thoughtful, single-player strategy game for anyone looking for a quick resource management game without decimal places. (Looking at you, Against the Storm.)

This is an interesting roguelite X citybuilder game - I'll give you that. Pros: 1. Beautiful hand-drawn art and music 2. Almost free of bugs 3. Roguelite adds an interesting twist on your normal city builder games 4. Core gameplay is deep. Cons: 1. This is more of a warning for citybuilder lovers who want to give it a try: The game is very selective on its target audience. Roguelite elements didn't really make the usually-hardcore gameplay from citybuilders easier to navigate - instead, it made it even harder to understand. The time limit forces players to make decisions fast with little to no room to make errors. So often times you learn your lessons by "losing your run", which can feel frustrating and "set back". This is very different from how players learn in city management games. In citybuilders there's rarely a rigid lose condition that says "you lost" - no, they're more lenient on that and usually "lose conditions" are soft conditions. And for citybuilders that do have a rigid lose condition, it only happens very scarcely. For example, in Frostpunk, although you can lose the game in various ways, they happen very slowly. If you have lost all support from your people, you would still be given an in-game-week or so as your "last chance", and then you would lose. Or, if your heat core is about to blow up, you can send workers in so that it can sustain itself a little longer. My point is, even if there are rigid lose conditions, they still give players some room to come back. However, if you mess it up at some point in your run in this game, most likely you're not gonna make it. I am a roguelite player and a strategy / citybuilder player, so for me I sort of enjoyed it. But I can imagine how players from either end could feel the frustration.

A really clever game, spicing up a lightweight base-builder with deck-building, run-based roguelite elements, light narrative reveals that are tied to gameplay in a low-stakes way, and a freeform way of unlocking permanent upgrades that mimics the core gameplay itself. You can see where it borrows some of its elements from, and I appreciate the way it incorporates them without feeling anything like the games that it learned from. There are a few quality-of-life things that I'd change (the inability to look at my whole deck when selecting a card to add or remove is frustrating at times, and once in a while building placement leaves me wishing that I had just a little more information, but stakes are low enough that the impact isn't that big anyway), but responsive devs, regular updates, and gameplay that clearly has the user in mind are all the green flags I want to see.

I think the designers may have good ideas but they don't have enough ability to make it come true. In a city building game I never feel so much pressure from the limited land use. Why the house can't be inherently designed as 1x1 so I don't need to always rotate it and can pay more attention to the other things. What's more, as a DBG game, Unless the cards have great advantages compare to the basic cards, A skillful players won't let it get into his deck. Sadly, numerical value of most cards in the game is just a trash. That's why the relics in the game are so powerful. You can even win the game with basic deck if you have good relics.

I don't know why this game is getting so little attention. It's a fun, lightweight deck-builder with a nice soundtrack and plenty of replayability. Some of the mechanics are a little opaque to me, but it wouldn't keep me from recommending the game.

This is my second favorite roguelike city builder after Against the Storm, but that one has beavers in raincoats so it's a pretty unfair contest. Still, I very much enjoy the Norse theme and the aesthetic that blends a rustic feel with touch of future-tech. The core mechanic of playing cards, placing buildings, and trying to generate resources effectively is very addicting, as is the meta progression. You can make some terribly fun combos with the right mix of artifacts and cards. The game is not perfect; for one, it needs a conclusion beyond finishing the quests. A simple "well done" from a god or two would go a long way in this economy. Two, it could use more maps: you'll see them all after a handful of runs. Three, it could also do a bit better at conveying threats and challenges. The risks of difficult maps are mixed in with your artifacts and buffs and can be very tiny if you have a lot. Also, when you use a card to spawn a threat, what spawned and where? The game isn't very clear on this. These are nitpicks, however. When I picked up the game, I wanted to keep playing until I was done and I was very satisfied throughout.

本作是一个纯粹经营向的DBG玩法的城建模拟游戏。不同于常见的类似Stackland之类的城建DBG范式，它们往往围绕一个村镇的基底进行长期和持续的建造，规划和升级。本作则是主要通过“闯关”的形式，不断更变场地进行破局。其核心就在于，你旅途的重点是带着你的维京长船进行冒险，而路途上的短程村建，则都是为了点亮世界树Yggdrasil散布在世界的根系，为自己的长船充能并旅行到下个地点。 游戏中没有战斗，而是一个非常数值向底层的经营玩法，你可以在地图的各处任意扩张。本作的基底建设机制很类似《岛民》，限制你建造建筑的，除了领土边界的扩张，就只有“周围需要的基础建筑”这一机制限制。你可以在每个回合无限制地制造基础设施民宅，为你提供1个人口。这张卡牌不会被消耗，但每次重复建造，其花费的资源都会变多，直到其性价比比不上其他建筑。而有了足够人口之后，你就可以建造兵营来提供武力，这将为你的边界扩张提供基础——别担心或是兴奋，这不意味着任何战斗，地块解锁也只是单纯的数值检查，游戏没有给玩家战略布局的玩法空间。你所要做的就是建立基础建筑，并在世界树树根的范围内建立满足其点亮条件的建筑。成功即过关，并到达新地图，游戏的核心挑战就是通过调优你的收益曲线，来在尽量少的回合数中点亮足够的树根来充能。 游戏的玩法核心其实算不上多薄弱，只不过确实有点过于平铺，缺乏随机性和挑战。游戏真正开始有趣起来要等到那个类Hades的自定义挑战热度系统开放，但这又需要过多的无随机性的标准流程，以及局外成长。但是游戏的美术则完全是iii的顶级水准，游戏以北欧神话作为背景，讲述了在诸神黄昏后，主角一行如何通过点亮世界树在各处的残存根系来重建九界。这个背景给了这个独特的关卡式4x城建一个扎实的剧情面的解释，重建九界的旅程也给了游戏中各种奇诡瑰丽的世界环境设计相当充分的美术设计空间。不仅各个人物都有细致的手绘风立绘，而且即使在讲解游戏机制的对话中也钩画了众人的性格。 总体而言，本作有着令人一眼即爱上的出色手绘美术，和一个尚算得上有趣的关卡式简化4x殖民地模拟玩法。可惜其选择的roguelike改进并没有和游戏的其他部分形成耦合，反而成了长线游玩中重复度的主因。 [quote]关注鉴赏组：[url=https://store.steampowered.com/curator/45134494]浮生评测[/url] ←"浮生若梦，一鉴倾心，邀您共赏人间烟火" 加入Steam组：[url=https://steamcommunity.com/groups/LLFLLFF]浮生评测[/url]←“一起追寻'浮生若梦'般的游戏体验” 开始“浮生若梦”鉴赏组的奇幻之旅！[/quote]

[h1] TLDR [/h1] Multiple strategic layers create engaging, complex play in this Norse-themed, deck-based, roguelike building game. Overly-random rolls affect choices, decks, outcomes and ultimately the fun factor. [h1] Intro[/h1] Roots of Yggdrasil is an enchanting game. It draws you in with its charming graphics and art style, calming soundtrack, and multiple layers where players can execute their strategies. At its heart, it is a city building game, with roguelike elements. You play the leader of a flying vessel, attempting to rebuild, after Ragnarok (the Norse apocalypse). By successfully completing missions, you gain the resources to power your ships (with seeds) and gain the resources necessary to upgrade your companions and your base (the Holt). Your companions grant you bonuses, both at the base, and while you’re attempting missions. Your missions (called “loops”) are timed; there is a black void chasing your vessel on the exploration map (the world tree, Yggdrasil) and the success of your missions is largely determined by how good your deck is – you gain cards through various means; quests during the missions, NPCs you encounter, etc. The exploration map is where you pick your next location for the mission. Once you land, you have to focus on quickly achieving side quests (to maximize the resources you gain on completion) while primarily trying to achieve the main quest (get enough seeds to power your ship; the number varies from level to level). Placement of your buildings is critical; one mistake, and you can be hooped down the road. There is no saving allowed (you only save when you return to the Holt) and you basically sink or swim during each mission without being able to try new tactics or building placement. There’s also no ready way to destroy existing buildings. If you exceed the time allotted for that mission, you will be penalized by getting cards with negative attributes (you can remove them, but at great cost). Once you decide to return to the Holt, another strategic layer emerges: you have to decide which resources you wish to exploit first, and thus which areas to clear. You need resources to do everything; clearing rubble, creating new buildings, etc. And you gain these resources when you successfully complete loops. Ok, let’s get to the nitty gritty: [h1] Likes [/h1] [b] + The multiple strategic layers in the game makes for engaging gameplay [/b] [b] + The lovely soundtrack is calming and quite hypnotic, especially during missions [/b] [b] + There is a fair amount of strategic depth at the exploration, Holt, and mission levels [/b] [b] + Learning the intricacies of your deck, which cards to get, which to discard, offers even more depth [/b] [h1] Dislikes[/h1] [b] - While there is a tutorial, the game is not very intuitive; you’re left wondering what you should be doing next, which resources are more valuable, etc. And the learning curve can be steep [/b] [b] - At the Holt, the game is not timed; when exploring, the time needed to reach a location is important but during a mission, timing is everything. This mechanism is a little too rigid in my opinion, and detracts from the fun you can have during a mission. After having to mostly grind your way, it becomes a little annoying as the penalties of missing deadlines stack up [/b] [b] - There’s too much randomness in this game. To be fair, some randomness can make a game more challenging but too much of it affects everything and unfairly increases the game’s difficulty: the deck you get, the cards that are drawn each round, the negative events that occur during a mission, the limited choices available in the exploration map, etc. [/b] [b] - I think the randomness is overly high and disadvantageous because they want you to fail, and keep trying. It’s this inherent structure of roguelikes that I generally dislike; I don’t like having to learn basic game mechanics by continuously failing and repeating [/b] [b] - Optimal placement of your structures is CRITICAL in this game (as it affects mission success). Unfortunately, you only learn this by making mistakes and realizing after; or failing, and trying again. I find this kind of “replay value” tiresome [/b] [h1] Verdict [/h1] The above QoL issues may not bother some players, but they bother me. I think having a mission clock should be used sparingly; if every mission is timed, it becomes a drudge. What’s the rush? Ragnarok is already over, right? Yes, it is a roguelike, so it can be argued that the game “should” be this way. But I think it would appeal to a wider audience if these elements can be refined somewhat and balanced better. In sum, Roots of Yggdrasil can be fun and could be even more so, if not for how roguelike features like timed missions and a high degree of randomness can drastically affect play-balancing and as such, the enjoyment of the game. 6.5/10.0

very slow to get into. i played most deck builders out there. this just isn't a deck builder it's a city buider, but instead of the buildigs, you're drawing cards that have the buildigs oon them. eery run feels the same, need housing, then barracks, then working camps etc. theres no optimization of combos. just requirements. regret buying it. im a sucker for rogue and deckbuilders. dont let the very postive review fool you. it only has 284 reviews total

Very solid! Having a home base whose meta-bonuses are based on the little city you build is a real highlight, and I'm really glad to see more faster paced, objective-driven city-builders. Overall the systems are combined well, but I wish the design was willing to get a little crazy with it. A lot of the cards and artifacts have built-in drawbacks that sort of dull what would make it enticing, and I just wasn't really interested in the ways that the game wanted to scale up its difficulty. But don't let those little nitpicks stop you! I enjoyed it and recommend it. Easy sale pickup.

Cozy and engaging roguelike deckbuilder/citybuilder. I'd give it a 7/10 at this point (tutorial and 1 loop completed). Pros: - Nice story (maybe a little light but I don't mind that) and cute, cozy graphics. - Plays well on my 15 year old computer. - Fairly engaging gameplay loop. Each stage of each loop feels a little like the first 20 minutes of a Civ or Age of Empires game. We'll see if it stays "fresh" as I ramp up in difficulty and # of Loops. - Retreads very old gameplay elements (roguelike with progression, building placement/engine building with exploration), but combines them in a fairly unique way. Cons: - Despite what it says, controller support is bugged to the point of being unusable. Right in the tutorial it wouldn't register any response when it prompted me to "press the top button". This is a really tough one to rate. An extremely fun concept and fantastic atmosphere with glacial metaprogression, and mildly clunky building controls while playing loops that become a massive hindrance when upgrading your base. It's a lot of fun playing loops, moving from island to island and carefully planning out an approach while simultaneously building my deck. The building controls are a little clunky, it's quite irritating fiddling with building placement to squeeze them into the best position. But runs are fairly dynamic and your deck and buffs can have a decent impact on how you play. Unfortunately outside of loops unlocks trickle in at an agonizing pace. Seeing the same cards over and over again is disappointing especially when it seems like there's a lot locked behind currencies that collect very slowly. This is extra frustrating due to runs taking well over an hour - finishing a run and unlocking maybe one or two tree upgrades is demoralizing. The building controls are just plain atrocious in the home base. Buildings are buried in a massive unsearchable hand of cards you have to mouse over one by one. You can't move placed buildings so if you need to relocate a group (proximity requirements force you to move them around a lot) you have to send them back to your hand as cards then find them again one by one. Building unlocks come just as slow as tree unlocks, but their impact is disappointing. +2% card rarity, +1 per loop of a resource you'll be spending hundreds of, etc. At the rate they're unlocking, I wonder if their impact will be significant after even 50 loops played. Even worse, they unlock via card packs so you have very little control over what you get. And the absolute cherry on top is that the packs that give you the resources you badly need (iron, trees - prereqs for many buildings) have a 50% chance to give you [b]useless cosmetic items[/b] instead. Atrocious home base mechanics aside, I really like the main gameplay. Runs feel dynamic and it oozes Norse mythological atmosphere. In the end I think this is an okay game that could be good with slightly better building controls and great with better metaprogression. Unfortunately nothing's likely to change with the game last being updated in the month of its release, over a year and a half ago. Tentatively recommended, but you should try the demo to see if the core gameplay will carry the day since the metaprogression will rarely do anything impactful.

I went back and forth on this one. I had a poor first impression, because the mechanics weren't clear to me. I warmed to it as I understood it better, but after running 4 expeditions ("loops") I got bored because each game seemed pretty much like the last one. Not enough changes between games, either in the kinds of maps you see or the upgrades you get from the meta-progression. It's a tile laying game with deck building mechanics. You build villages on floating islands, with the goal of blooming 2-3 trees on each one and then getting off before the creeping darkness kills you. You're mostly doing two things, building up your Supply income and increasing your Might. Almost all cards cost Supply to play, and to expand your village, you need to spend Might to unlock new zones on the island. Every game plays pretty much the same. You start with in a cramped area, play a bunch of houses, and then play a couple of Barracks to gain one-time Might awards from those houses so you can unlock new zones. Once you've got some room, you place mines and logging camps to increase your Supply income. As your population grows, you draft more cards. Some of these are better mines and logging camps, some are cards that give you actual Might income instead of one-time awards, and some give you Supply income from housing but have various prerequisites. As you expand across the island, you encounter magic trees that you need to bloom. Each has specific requirements, like place so many houses nearby, or so many Might or support buildings. It's interesting enough the first few times, but it gets really repetitive. Despite every map being randomly generated, they end up feeling much the same. There are 3-4 different kinds of islands, and you tend to see them in the same order in every game. There's some meta-progression where you unlock rewards that improve each run, but the rewards are so small and trivial they feel like they don't matter at all.

Roots of Yggdrasil is a difficult game for me to review. At its core it's a turn-based city building Roguelike deckbuilder. It's got all the hallmarks - runs, meta progression, story that you unlock piece by piece, etc. The art style is really charming and the gameplay works really well. The story so far is interesting, if a little played out in terms of the subject matter. It's a great time killer and in general runs don't take too long. It's significantly more relaxed than the average roguelike. However, there are several things that annoy me with this game and encouraged me to put it down. The metaprogression is sloooooooow. You do 3-4 runs to unlock the ability to start the game with 1 extra resource (which is 1/5 of the cost of most buildings). The story progression (at least when tied to the characters) is gated behind adding difficulty modifiers to your runs very early on. Also there is a clearly best option for a "hero" - the one that gets to blop down a free building every few turns. The others don't even compare, but you need to take them along to progress their story. Essentially adding another difficulty modifier for yourself The variety is not really there - the maps are fairly similar, the objectives are all the same and the cards are mostly pretty boring. Runs barely differ from each other and when they do, it's essentially by the end of the run. I don't know if it's the number of cards or how weak the artifacts are, but something is off about it. With all those things together, Roots of Yggdrasil pretty quickly becomes samey and rather boring. To a degree, this is the "fault" of the Roguelike genre, but it just feels like something is missing here. I wouldn't really recommend it unless you really want the novelty of a city-building Roguelike.
